entries.name: Bubble Sort
entries.problem: Orders a short list of comparable values by repeatedly swapping out-of-order neighbors.
entries.intuition: Imagine shaking a list so adjacent items compare and the heavier ones slowly drift to the end each pass.
entries.inputs: Array or list of comparable elements.
entries.outputs: Same collection arranged in non-decreasing order.
steps: Start at the first index.
Compare the current element with the next element.
Swap if the pair is out of order.
Move one position forward and repeat until the pass ends.
Shrink the unsorted tail and loop until a pass produces no swaps.
entries.time_complexity: O(n²) average/worst, O(n) best when already sorted.
strengths: Simple to code and reason about.
Detects nearly-sorted input quickly if optimized to stop early.
weaknesses: Quadratic runtime makes it impractical for medium or large inputs.
Performs many redundant comparisons.
entries.explanation: Keep comparing neighbors so misplaced values crawl to the edges; repeat until no swaps happen.

entries.name: Insertion Sort
entries.problem: Maintains a growing sorted prefix by inserting each new value into its proper place.
entries.intuition: Like sorting playing cards: keep the hand sorted and slide each new card into position.
entries.inputs: Array or list of comparable items.
entries.outputs: Same collection sorted in ascending order.
steps: Treat the first element as sorted.
Pick the next element (the key).
Shift larger elements in the sorted prefix one step to the right.
Insert the key into the freed slot.
Advance to the next element and repeat until the array is consumed.
entries.time_complexity: O(n²) average/worst, O(n) best on nearly-sorted data.
strengths: Excellent on tiny or almost sorted datasets.
weaknesses: Quadratic when many elements are out of order.
Heavy shifting work for long lists.
entries.explanation: Grow a sorted prefix and carefully insert each new element where it belongs.

entries.name: Selection Sort
entries.problem: Sorts by repeatedly selecting the smallest remaining element and placing it at the front.
entries.intuition: Scan the pile for the tiniest card, put it next in line, and continue with the leftovers.
entries.inputs: Array or list of comparable values.
steps: Set the current position i to 0.
Find the smallest element from i to end.
Swap that element with position i.
Increment i and repeat until the list is ordered.
entries.example: [7, 3, 5] → smallest is 3, swap with 7 ⇒ [3, 7, 5]; next smallest is 5, swap ⇒ [3, 5, 7].
strengths: Easy to reason about and implement.
weaknesses: Still quadratic in comparisons.
Not stable without extra work.
entries.explanation: Repeatedly locate the smallest unused value and stick it at the next slot of the sorted prefix.

entries.name: Merge Sort
entries.problem: Efficiently sorts large lists by divide-and-conquer merging of sorted halves.
entries.intuition: Split the deck until each pile has one card, then merge piles back together in order.
entries.inputs: Array or list of comparable elements.
steps: Divide the array into two halves.
Recursively sort each half.
Merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front element.
Continue merging until a single sorted list remains.
entries.time_complexity: O(n log n) for all cases.
strengths: Great for linked lists and external sorting.
weaknesses: Requires extra memory for merging.
Recursive overhead on constrained environments.
entries.explanation: Keep splitting into halves until singles, then merge each pair while keeping them sorted.

entries.name: Quick Sort
entries.problem: Efficient in-place sort that partitions around a pivot and recursively sorts partitions.
entries.intuition: Pick a pivot, move smaller items left and larger right, then repeat on the two sides.
entries.outputs: Array sorted ascending or descending based on comparator.
steps: Choose a pivot element.
Partition the array so items < pivot go left, > pivot go right.
Recursively quick sort the left partition.
Recursively quick sort the right partition.
Concatenate left + pivot + right segments.
entries.time_complexity: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst if pivots are poor.
weaknesses: Worst-case quadratic when pivots are unbalanced.
Not stable by default.
entries.explanation: Divide around an intelligently chosen pivot so the partitions shrink quickly, leading to near-logarithmic depth.

entries.name: Heap Sort
entries.problem: Sorts by turning the input into a heap and repeatedly extracting the max (or min).
entries.intuition: Build a priority queue so the largest element can be removed and placed at the end one by one.
steps: Heapify the entire array (build max-heap).
Swap the root (largest value) with the last element.
Reduce the heap size by one and heapify the root.
Repeat extraction and heapify until one element remains.
entries.example: [4, 1, 3, 2] → build max-heap [4,2,3,1] → swap 4/1 ⇒ [1,2,3,4]; heapify remaining ⇒ [3,2,1,4] → continue until sorted.
entries.time_complexity: O(n log n) for all cases.
entries.space_complexity: O(1) extra space besides recursion-free heapify.
weaknesses: Not stable.
Constant factors higher than quick sort on average.
entries.explanation: Leverage the heap property so the largest item is always on top, remove it, and restore the heap repeatedly.

entries.name: Counting Sort
entries.problem: Sorts integers from a limited range by counting occurrences instead of comparing.
entries.intuition: Count how many times each value appears, then rebuild the list in order using counts as guides.
entries.inputs: List of integers within a known small range.
entries.outputs: Stable sorted list of the same integers.
steps: Determine the min and max values.
Allocate a counts array covering the range.
Tally each element’s frequency.
Optionally convert counts to prefix sums for stability.
Write elements back in order using the counts.
entries.time_complexity: O(n + k) where k is range size.
strengths: Linear time when k ≪ n log n.
Stable if prefix sums are used.
weaknesses: Requires known, limited range.
Extra memory proportional to range size.
entries.explanation: Use frequency counts rather than comparisons, making it lightning-fast on bounded integer domains.

entries.name: Radix Sort
entries.problem: Sorts integers or fixed-length strings by processing digits from least to most significant (or vice versa).
entries.intuition: Group numbers by each digit place using a stable sorter so positions eventually align globally.
steps: Choose digit order (LSB-first for integers).
For each digit position:
- Group elements by digit using a stable bucket (like counting sort).
- Concatenate buckets to reform the list.
Stop once the most significant digit is processed.
entries.example: [170, 45, 75, 90] ⇒ bucket by units, then tens, then hundreds ⇒ [45, 75, 90, 170].
entries.time_complexity: O(d · (n + k)) where d is digit count and k bucket size.
weaknesses: Needs stable sub-sorting and uniform key lengths.
Extra memory for buckets.
entries.explanation: Repeatedly bucket by digit so that by the final pass the entire key ordering emerges.

entries.name: Bucket Sort
entries.problem: Sorts uniformly distributed real numbers by scattering them into buckets and sorting each bucket.
entries.intuition: Partition the [0,1) range into buckets so each holds a small local list that can be sorted quickly.
entries.inputs: List of real numbers typically normalized to [0, 1).
steps: Create k empty buckets.
Distribute each element into the appropriate bucket based on value.
Sort individual buckets (often using insertion sort).
Concatenate the buckets in order.
entries.time_complexity: Average O(n) when distribution is uniform; worst O(n²) if items clump.
strengths: Buckets can be processed in parallel.
weaknesses: Performance degrades on skewed data.
Requires knowledge of value distribution.
entries.explanation: Exploit the distribution shape so each bucket is tiny, making local sorts trivial.

entries.name: Linear Search
entries.problem: Finds the position of a target value by scanning elements sequentially.
entries.intuition: Check each item in order until the desired one appears or the list ends.
entries.outputs: Index of the target or -1 if absent.
steps: Start at index 0.
Compare current element with target.
If equal, return the index.
Otherwise advance to the next index.
Stop after the final element and return -1 if not found.
entries.time_complexity: O(n) average and worst; O(1) best if first element matches.
strengths: Simple to implement and reason about.
weaknesses: Slow on large datasets due to full scan.
Cannot skip work without extra structure.
entries.explanation: Walk through each entry until the goal appears; trivial but potentially time-consuming.

entries.name: Binary Search
entries.problem: Finds a target in a sorted list by repeatedly halving the search interval.
entries.intuition: Like guessing a number: choose the midpoint, discard the half where the answer cannot live, repeat.
entries.outputs: Index of target or -1 if missing.
steps: Set low and high pointers to the bounds.
Compute mid = (low + high) // 2.
If array[mid] equals target, return mid.
If target < array[mid], move high to mid - 1.
Else move low to mid + 1 and repeat until low > high.
entries.example: Search 9 in [1,3,5,7,9,11]: mid=5→value=7 < 9, shift low ⇒ new mid=9 found at index 4.
strengths: Very fast on massive sorted arrays.
weaknesses: Requires sorted data with random access.
Insertion/deletion may break order.
entries.explanation: Keep cutting the remaining range in half so the number of candidates collapses exponentially.

entries.name: Jump Search
entries.problem: Balances linear and binary search by jumping ahead fixed blocks in a sorted array.
entries.intuition: Skip ahead in strides; once you overshoot, do a short linear scan backward.
steps: Choose optimal step ≈ √n.
Jump ahead by step size until value ≥ target or end reached.
Perform linear search backward within the block where target could reside.
Return index if found, else -1.
entries.example: [1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15], target 9, step=2: jump indices 0→2→4 (value 9) stop and confirm.
strengths: Fewer comparisons than linear search on sorted data.
weaknesses: Still slower than binary search.
Requires random access to jump.
entries.explanation: Hop through the array in fixed leaps, then crawl a short distance to find the exact slot.

entries.name: Interpolation Search
entries.problem: Searches uniformly distributed sorted data by estimating the likely position of the target.
entries.intuition: Instead of always probing the middle, interpolate where the target might land based on value range.
entries.inputs: Sorted list with roughly uniform distribution and the target.
steps: Maintain low and high indices.
Estimate pos = low + (target - arr[low]) * (high - low) / (arr[high] - arr[low]).
If arr[pos] equals target, return pos.
If target < arr[pos], move high to pos - 1; else move low to pos + 1.
Repeat until low > high or value found.
entries.example: In [10,20,30,40,50], searching 40 calculates pos near index 3 immediately.
entries.time_complexity: O(log log n) average on uniform data, O(n) worst if distribution is skewed.
strengths: Fewer probes than binary search on uniform keys.
weaknesses: Performance collapses on clustered data.
Requires numeric keys with known range.
entries.explanation: Guess where the target should live based on proportional distance, probe there, and tighten the bounds.

entries.name: SQL Queries
entries.problem: Retrieve, filter, and manipulate relational data using declarative statements.
entries.intuition: Describe the desired result set while the optimizer chooses an execution plan.
entries.outputs: Result set, affected row count, or updated storage state.
steps: Parse the SQL statement.
Validate against schema and permissions.
Generate a logical plan (joins, filters, projections).
Optimize into a physical plan using indexes and statistics.
Execute the plan and stream results back to the client.
entries.example: SELECT name FROM customers WHERE country='Canada'; returns matching customer names.
entries.time_complexity: Varies; indexed lookups approach O(log n), full scans O(n).
entries.space_complexity: Driven by execution plan (temporary joins, sorting buffers).
strengths: Mature optimizers leverage indexes and caches.
weaknesses: Poorly written queries can degrade to full scans.
Requires understanding of indexes and statistics for tuning.
entries.explanation: State what data you want, let the relational engine decide how to fetch it efficiently.

entries.name: SQL Joins
entries.problem: Combine rows from related tables based on matching keys.
entries.intuition: Treat tables like sets and match rows where keys agree or complement each other.
entries.inputs: Two or more tables plus join condition.
entries.outputs: Composite rows containing columns from each source table.
steps: Choose join type (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS).
Identify join keys/conditions.
Relational engine decides join algorithm (nested loop, hash, merge).
Execute join, producing combined tuples.
Apply downstream filters or projections.
entries.example: SELECT orders.id, customers.name FROM orders INNER JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id;
entries.time_complexity: Depends on join algorithm; hash join ~O(n + m), nested loop ~O(n·m) without indexes.
entries.space_complexity: May require hash tables or sort buffers.
strengths: Expressive way to relate normalized tables.
weaknesses: Expensive if keys lack indexes.
Incorrect join types can duplicate or drop rows.
entries.explanation: Map matching keys across tables so related data can be viewed as a single combined set.

entries.name: SQL Transactions
entries.problem: Bundle multiple statements into an atomic, consistent, isolated, durable unit of work.
entries.intuition: Either all operations succeed together or none do, safeguarding integrity even under failures.
entries.outputs: Committed data changes or a rollback to the previous state.
steps: BEGIN (implicit or explicit) starts a transaction context.
Execute one or more SQL statements.
If all succeed, issue COMMIT to persist changes.
On error or manual cancel, issue ROLLBACK to undo.
DBMS enforces ACID properties via logging and locking.
entries.example: Transfer funds: debit one account, credit another, COMMIT only if both succeed; else ROLLBACK.
entries.time_complexity: Depends on enclosed statements; logging adds small overhead.
entries.space_complexity: Requires log space for redo/undo records.
strengths: Protects data integrity under concurrency and crashes.
weaknesses: Excessive transaction scope can cause contention.
Long transactions hold locks, reducing throughput.
entries.explanation: Group related statements so they behave as a single all-or-nothing change, ensuring ACID guarantees.
